The Vagrant shrew (Sorex vagrans), a small soricid mammal inhabiting moist meadows and coniferous forests of western North America, exhibits a reproductive strategy characterized by relatively low annual output. A typical litter contains between two and eight pups [N_R_i = litter contains between two and eight pups], and females produce only a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], a rate that is modest for an insectivore of its size. Neonates weigh a mere half gram at birth (0.5 grams) [Wwb = 0.5 grams], reflecting the extreme altricial state of soricid newborns, which are born hairless and entirely dependent on maternal care. The gestation period is short, lasting only twenty days [tg = twenty days] when measured at a maternal body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a value consistent with the high metabolic demands of maintaining pregnancy in a mammal with a rapid life history. This abbreviated intrauterine development is offset by an extended period of post-natal investment, during which the altricial pups undergo significant growth and physiological maturation before achieving nutritional independence.

Weaning, marking the transition from a milk-based diet to independent foraging, occurs at approximately thirty days [tx = approximately thirty days] after birth under a normal developmental temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. At this point, the young shrews have typically reached a wet body mass of approximately 5.5 grams [Wwx = approximately 5.5 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase over birth weight and indicating a phase of rapid mass gain during the suckling period. This weaning weight is still modest, however, and the juveniles must continue to refine their foraging skills while avoiding predation from larger mammals and avian raptors. The subsequent juvenile stage is a period of continued growth and behavioral development, as the sub-adult individuals gradually acquire the proficiency needed to capture the invertebrate prey that constitutes their primary diet. The time invested in gestation and lactation combined is modest relative to the total lifespan, allowing for a rapid generational turnover in favorable environments, a characteristic life-history pattern among small-bodied soricids.

Puberty in Sorex vagrans is not reached until well after the juvenile stage has concluded, with gonadal maturation occurring at 417 days [tp = 417 days] after birth when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This protracted period to sexual maturity, exceeding one year, is a notable feature for a mammal of such small body size, and it likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a high mass-specific metabolic rate and the challenges of resource acquisition in seasonally variable temperate habitats. The delay until reproductive activation ensures that individuals have attained sufficient body size and physiological condition to support the costs of gestation and lactation. Upon reaching adulthood, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown Vagrant shrew is approximately 7 grams [Wwi = approximately 7 grams], though field records indicate a typical range of 4 to 8 grams depending on sex, season, and local food availability. This asymptotic mass places Sorex vagrans among the smaller members of its genus, with correspondingly high energetic demands per unit of body mass.

The species exhibits a relatively high resting metabolic rate, a direct consequence of its small size and active lifestyle. Basal oxygen consumption has been measured at 28.1 milliliters per hour [JOi = 28.1 milliliters per hour] when the shrew is at an ambient temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a value that underscores the intense energetic costs of maintaining endothermy in a tiny mammal. This metabolic rate, which is among the highest recorded for mammals of comparable mass, necessitates a near-constant foraging effort to meet daily caloric requirements; shrews must consume a large proportion of their body weight in food each day or risk starvation. The high metabolic engine powers a rapid life cycle, but it also imposes constraints on lifespan, as the cumulative physiological wear from sustained high output can accelerate senescence. The interplay between metabolic investment and longevity is a central theme in understanding the life-history evolution of this species.

Maximum recorded longevity for the Vagrant shrew in the wild is approximately 2 years [am = approximately 2 years] under conditions that include a core body temperature near 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a lifespan that is typical for a mammal of this body size but short in absolute terms. This brief existence is characterized by a single reproductive season for most individuals, as the combination of a late puberty and a single annual litter constrains total lifetime fecundity. The intensive pace of life, from the rapid neonatal growth and short gestation to the high metabolic expenditure, is a classic example of a "fast" life-history strategy adapted to environments where adult mortality is high and unpredictable. Field studies suggest that few individuals survive to a second winter, with most mortality concentrated during the first few months after weaning when juveniles face the greatest risks from predation and resource competition. The species compensates for its short lifespan by maintaining high physiological performance throughout its active period.
